findings.why: The headline's 8% sits next to 'Glycolic' and '[Melasyl + Niacinamide]', but the body states 1% Glycolic Acid and 2% Niacinamide. No listed ingredient is at 8%, so the headline overstates the strength in the bottle.
findings.fix: Glycolic Bright Face Serum with 1% Glycolic Acid + 2% Niacinamide + Melasyl; if 8% is a blend total, say so and list each ingredient's strength.

findings.span: helps fade dark spots in as little as 4 weeks
findings.why: A result promised within 4 weeks needs a study of that duration, and its qualifier (what was measured, on how many people) must be on the ad; none is shown.
findings.fix: Keep it only with the study footnote on the creative; otherwise: 'helps fade the look of dark spots with continued use'.

findings.why: 'Skin renewal' means cell turnover, a body process, so claiming to support it is a structure/function claim for legal to clear. It is fine if reworded to the exfoliation the ad already describes.

rule_hit_review.why: 1% Glycolic Acid is stated twice in the body and reads as the true per-ingredient strength; the real mismatch is the headline's 'Glycolic Bright 8%', raised as a finding. Don't 'fix' this line to 8%.
2% Niacinamide is stated consistently in the body; the conflict is the headline's unattributed '8% [Melasyl + Niacinamide]', raised as a finding. Confirm against the label.
Repeat of the 1% Glycolic Acid statement, consistent with the first; the problem is the headline's 8%.
Repeat of the 2% Niacinamide statement, consistent with the first; the problem is the headline's 8%.

tone_read: This is the closest of these ads to Minimalist's register: calm and hedged ('help visibly reduce', 'more even-looking complexion', 'over time'), with usage steps and a named mechanism (AHA exfoliation). It slips into mood words in places ('naturally luminous', 'radiant') but has no fear hooks or hype.
language_read: The body states concentrations in the brand's format (1% Glycolic Acid, 2% Niacinamide), but the headline's unattributed '8%' contradicts them and Melasyl has no strength at all. Efficacy is mostly scoped correctly, apart from the time-bound 'in as little as 4 weeks' with no qualifier.
